environment.label: Environmental history
environment.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts. Dust Bowl debates distinguish agricultural capitalism, technology and soils, federal intervention, regional scale and household survival; primary criticism and later social history complicate a single causal summary.
environment.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

environment.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.

strands.title: Unequal pollution burdens and collective action
strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.
strands.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), selected reprinted excerpts

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes
strands.focus: Worster argues for interacting natural and cultural forces while emphasizing agricultural capitalism. McDean criticizes his generalization, contests Bonnifield’s federal-policy account and favors Hurt’s regional specificity. These are competing interpretations.
strands.works: Worster (1986); McDean (1986), discussing books of 1979 and 1981

strands.title: Ecological adaptation and the promise of development
strands.focus: Worster acknowledges Malin’s ecological history but disputes explanations through natural storms and a passing pioneering stage. He distinguishes rival cultural values and varied regional entrepreneurial intensity.

strands.title: Regional boundaries and histories of staying
strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.

strands.title: Wilderness, livelihood and different political contexts
strands.focus: Guha targets American deep ecology’s universal claims and conservation’s unequal costs in India, while acknowledging Naess’s concern about inequality. Cronon studies American sublime/frontier ideals and everyday responsibility, explicitly citing Guha in note28. Shared concerns about exclusion do not erase their different contexts or Cronon’s support for protected wild lands.

strands.title: Can biocentrism incorporate social criticism?
strands.focus: Johns’s abstract disputes Guha’s equation of deep ecology with wilderness protection and defends biocentrism joined to critical social theory against overconsumption and militarism. This is a named response; the article’s detailed reasoning is not newly verified.

strands.title: Cultural criticism and habitat protection
strands.focus: Sessions objects that Cronon underweights biodiversity and connected wild habitat. His claim that cultural construction conflicts with independent nature is a critical interpretation: Cronon explicitly defends nonhuman autonomy and wild-land protection.

strands.title: Material change, ideas and gendered nature
strands.focus: Merchant retrospectively clarifies that ecological and economic changes made some ideas more plausible rather than mechanically causing them. Her socialist ecofeminism addresses production and reproduction and challenges an essentialist identification of women with nature.
strands.works: The Death of Nature (1980); Radical Ecology (1992), discussed in Merchant’s 2006 retrospective

strands.title: Colonial conservation: knowledge, power and benefits
strands.focus: Carruthers’s review welcomes Grove’s island settings and exchanges of knowledge, while questioning parts of his synthesis. Her Kruger prologue and epilogue emphasize changing political coalitions, racial exclusion and allocation of benefits. Scientific conservation and unequal power can coexist; these works ask different questions at different scales.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995), reviewed by Carruthers (1996); The Kruger National Park (1995), prologue and epilogue

global.label: World / global / connected history
global.description: Moves across national containers through comparison, interaction, circulation, and connections. These approaches differ; global scale need not imply one theory of globalization.
global.representative_figures_and_works: William McNeill (1963); Eric Wolf (1982); Sanjay Subrahmanyam (1997); Kenneth Pomeranz (2000).

strands.focus: Hodgson contests maps and a single Western mainstream; the later edited collection transmits earlier essays.

strands.title: Cross-cultural encounters and religious change
strands.focus: Conversion, conflict and compromise are historical processes requiring conditions of contact.

strands.title: Eurasian states, economies and popular action
strands.focus: Economic similarities and political differences require distinct comparisons; European categories need historical testing.

strands.title: Imperial networks and political imagination

strands.title: Comparison and connection in dispute

strands.title: Reciprocal comparison and connected units

strands.title: Proto-industry and the limits of trade
strands.focus: Pomeranz extends Mokyr’s labor model across regions while questioning unlimited manufacture exports and resource imports at unchanged relative prices. Comparing regions also requires examining their trading partners.

indigenous.label: Indigenous history & decolonizing methods
indigenous.date_label: Earlier examples 1615–1938; 1970s–90s growth · baseline through 2000; selected 2010 intervention
indigenous.description: Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and scholarly research meet in varied academic practices. Oral histories, family relationships, archival inquiry and collaborations contribute different resources; authority and methods remain situated.
indigenous.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier selected writing includes Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), and Cree/Tainui interwar work. Twentieth-century examples include McNickle (1949), Deloria (1969), Adams and LaRocque (1975), Dickason (1984, 1992), Sioui (1989), Walker (1990), Kameʻeleihiwa (1992), O’Brien (1997), Wilson (1996), and Smith (1999). See the distinct approaches for works, collaborators and evidence limits. Related scholarship includes Miller, White, Harris and Lutz; Stó:lō field-school practice credits community and university participants. Leddy’s 2010 reflection supplies a separately dated later case.

indigenous.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

science.label: History of science
science.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches · coverage through 2000
science.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
science.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

strands.focus: Yates and Rossi investigate historically situated methods; the Vickers volume questions simple transitions and proposes distinctions. Neither occult unity nor its direct transformation into all modern science is assumed.
strands.works: Yates, The Art of Memory (1966), chapter XVII; Rossi, Clavis universalis (1960); Vickers, ed., Occult and Scientific Mentalities (1984)

strands.title: Human sciences, classifications and professions
strands.focus: Foucault’s questions about objects and institutions meet Goldstein’s historical analysis of psychiatric professionalization; the profile reports productive empirical revision, not automatic application.
strands.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); Console and Classify (1987)

strands.title: Images and historical forms of objectivity
strands.focus: Mechanical restraint is one historically situated ideal, distinct from a claim to truth or escape from every perspective.

strands.title: Instruments and coordination
strands.focus: Galison’s project examines how apparatus and shared work connect different technical traditions.

strands.title: Arabic mathematics and conceptual history
strands.focus: Rashed examines configurations and transformations within mathematical knowledge.

strands.title: Colonial Indian science
strands.focus: Kumar’s project addresses administration, education, research and Indian responses.

strands.title: Endogenous knowledge and research priorities
strands.focus: Hountondji challenges the treatment of inherited knowledge as timeless.

strands.title: African health and healing histories
strands.focus: Distinct medical traditions are examined in historical and social settings.
strands.works: The Social Basis of Health and Healing in Africa (1992)

strands.title: Normal science, criticism and research programmes
strands.focus: Kuhn’s puzzle-solving emphasis, Popper’s defense of critical training and Lakatos’s programme appraisal are competing positions.
strands.works: Kuhn and Popper contributions (1970); Lakatos radio talk (1973)

strands.title: Bacon’s metaphors and experimental power
strands.focus: Pesic’s 1999 abstract reads Proteus as mutual struggle and testing. Merchant’s later response distinguishes literal wording from rhetorical legitimation: she agrees Bacon did not write the familiar torture phrases, yet defends her domination argument. Competing interpretations remain explicit.
strands.works: The Death of Nature (1980); “Wrestling with Proteus” (1999); Merchant (2006), retrospective response

science.scope_note: Kuhn is a central reorientation, not the field’s sole founder. Sarton, Koyré, Merton, and historians of experimental practice distinguish important approaches; Yates and Foucault are additional contributions. Chinese science and women’s scientific work expand this selection; it still needs fuller coverage of other regions and material practices. Named Chinese-series contributors and Daston/Galison’s image and instrument studies deepen the selection. Publication credits do not replace primary argument checks; wider regional coverage remains selective. Arabic mathematics, colonial Indian science, African healing and a Beninese knowledge programme are separate selected projects, not regional proxies or exhaustive coverage.

urbanhistory.label: Urban history
urbanhistory.date_label: Earlier city histories · postwar expansion · Urban History Yearbook 1974 · coverage through 2000
urbanhistory.description: Studies cities and urbanization through institutions, populations, built environments and connections beyond city boundaries. Local reconstruction, quantitative mobility research, colonial spatial analysis and histories of segregation or public landscapes form different approaches.
urbanhistory.representative_figures_and_works: H. J. Dyos: Urban History Yearbook programme (1974); Sam Bass Warner Jr.: Streetcar Suburbs (1962; second edition 1978); Stephan Thernstrom: Poverty and Progress (1964); Thomas J. Sugrue: The Origins of the Urban Crisis (1996); Anthony D. King: Colonial Urban Development (1976); William Cronon: Nature’s Metropolis (1991); Dolores Hayden: The Power of Place (1995); Lynn Hollen Lees: “The challenge of political change” (1994). David Harvey: Social Justice and the City (1973); Walter Benjamin: Das Passagen-Werk (1982); Michel de Certeau: “Walking in the City” (1980).

representative_people.context: Organizes a British and international urban-history community, as Reeder’s 1979 appreciation records.
representative_people.works: Urban History Yearbook programme (1974)

representative_people.context: Studies the making of Boston suburbs through transport and building.
representative_people.works: Streetcar Suburbs (1962; second edition 1978)

representative_people.context: Uses linked local records to investigate mobility while raising representativeness as a problem.
representative_people.works: Poverty and Progress (1964)

representative_people.context: Connects racial exclusion, institutions and industrial restructuring in Detroit.
representative_people.works: The Origins of the Urban Crisis (1996)

representative_people.context: Examines colonial spatial arrangements and social power, particularly Delhi.
representative_people.works: Colonial Urban Development (1976)

representative_people.context: Relates urban markets and processing to rural resources and production.
representative_people.works: Nature’s Metropolis (1991)

representative_people.context: Connects urban landscapes and public historical interpretation.
representative_people.works: The Power of Place (1995)

representative_people.context: Questions restricted urban biographies and the relative neglect of politics.
representative_people.works: “The challenge of political change” (1994)

representative_people.context: Geographer whose urban political economy and historical studies of the city are standard resources for urban historians. A contributor from geography, not a school member.
representative_people.works: Social Justice and the City (1973); The Condition of Postmodernity (1989)

representative_people.context: The unfinished Passagen-Werk on nineteenth-century Paris is a central resource for cultural histories of the city, its arcades and commodities. His Frankfurt and memory contexts remain.
representative_people.works: Das Passagen-Werk (1982); The Arcades Project (1999)

representative_people.context: “Walking in the City” gives urban historians a vocabulary of spatial practice and everyday use. His practice-theory context remains.
representative_people.works: The Practice of Everyday Life (1980; English 1984)

urbanhistory.scope_note: British institution-building and US quantitative urban studies do not define one school or exhaust the field. Cities are not self-contained units. Delhi adds a specific colonial inquiry; wider Asian, African, Latin American and medieval/early-modern historiographies remain underrepresented. Journal milestones mark consolidation, not the first historical study of cities.

strands.title: Field organization and methodological debate
strands.focus: Dyos’s community-building and Lees’s later criticism show an open, contested research field.

strands.title: Transport, building and suburbs
strands.focus: Warner’s Boston case links infrastructure and the development of residential space.

strands.title: Urban mobility and linked records
strands.focus: Thernstrom tests mobility through census, tax and other local records.

strands.title: Race and industrial change
strands.focus: Sugrue studies exclusion and deindustrialization through Detroit institutions.
strands.works: The Origins of the Urban Crisis (1996)

strands.title: Colonial power and urban space
strands.focus: King’s Delhi study examines spatial arrangements as expressions of social and political power.

strands.title: Cities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Cronon follows commodities between rural production and urban processing and exchange.

strands.title: Public landscapes and interpretation
strands.focus: Hayden connects place-based interpretation with urban social histories.

strands.title: Space, capital and the cultural city
strands.focus: Urban political economy (Harvey), the city of arcades and commodities (Benjamin) and spatial practice (de Certeau) supply the spatial and cultural turn in urban history, beside the entry’s social-science programme. They are resources from geography, criticism and theory, not a school.
strands.works: Social Justice and the City (1973); Das Passagen-Werk (1982); The Practice of Everyday Life (1980/84)
